title: Theory of Airy-Beam Wavefront Sensing
abstract: A new wavefront sensing framework based on the interference of counter-accelerating Airy beams is presented. An engineered cubic phase function transforms a single Gaussian beam into two coherent Airy beams with opposite transverse accelerations, which self-recombine during free-space propagation to form an interference pattern encoding the aberrated incident wavefront. Numerical simulations demonstrate accurate recovery of the aberrated exit-pupil phase across the aberration sets considered, with a root-mean-square phase reconstruction error below $10^{-6} \mathrm{\;rad}$ for the aberration set shown and consistently low errors for the other sets, while maintaining accurate recovery in the presence of measurement noise. The approach eliminates collection optics and enables a compact wavefront-sensing architecture for applications where conventional interferometric systems are difficult to implement, including electron-optical systems, augmented and virtual reality systems.
summary: This paper presents a novel, compact wavefront sensing technique utilizing the interference of counter-accelerating Airy beams. By encoding the unknown exit-pupil aberration into the relative phase of the interference pattern, the method allows for highly accurate phase reconstruction. This eliminates bulky collection optics, making it ideal for integrating wavefront sensing into complex systems like electron-optical or AR/VR devices.
main_problem: To develop a wavefront sensing framework that accurately reconstructs unknown aberrations in an exit pupil without requiring conventional collection optics.
main_result: The proposed method achieves accurate phase reconstruction with an RMS error below $10^{-6}$ rad, demonstrating high performance even in the presence of measurement noise.
method: The technique uses the interference pattern generated by two coherent Airy beams, derived from a single Gaussian beam via an engineered cubic phase function, and measures the resulting phase shift using a four-step phase-shifting interferometry scheme.
model_or_system: The system models the propagation of light through an aberrated exit pupil, encoding the aberration into the relative phase difference ($\Delta\psi$) measured in the Fourier plane via the interference of counter-accelerating Airy beams.
key_observables: The resulting interference pattern intensity $I_\delta(r)$ and the wrapped relative phase $\Delta\psi_{	ext{wrap}}$ obtained from the four-step measurement.
important_parameters: The aberration is parameterized by low-order coefficients (e.g., defocus, astigmatism, spherical aberration).
main_assumptions: The reconstruction relies on solving an inverse problem using the full wave-optical forward model, although a local relationship approximation is also discussed.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the conceptual architecture (Fig. 1), the phase-shearing pattern due to aberrations (Fig. 2), and the four-step phase-shifting interferometry scheme (Fig. 3).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical setup using cubic phase elements to generate Airy beams, details the four-step phase measurement process, formulates the aberration recovery as an inverse problem, and presents numerical simulations validating the reconstruction accuracy and noise tolerance.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems because it proposes a compact, non-interferometric method for measuring complex phase structures (aberrations) that can be crucial for high-precision quantum state preparation or quantum sensing applications.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Conceptual architecture of the proposed Airy-beam wavefront sensor. A Gaussian beam illuminates an aberrated exit pupil containing the optical phase structure of the system. An engineered cubic-phase element generates two coherent channels with opposite cubic phase. The corresponding Airy fields propagate to the Fourier plane, where they interfere and the resulting intensity is recorded for phase recovery.

Fig. 2. Interference of the conjugate cubic-phase channels with- out and with exit-pupil aberrations. The aberrated case in- cludes −2 waves of defocus, 3 waves of astigmatism, and 10 waves of spherical aberration. A visible phase-shearing pat- tern appears in the interference phase in the presence of aber- rations.

Fig. 3. Four-step interferometric phase retrieval in the Fourier plane for a wavefront containing 10λ spherical aberration, −2λ defocus, and 3λ astigmatism. Four intensity measure- ments are acquired with controlled relative phase shifts of 0, π/2, π, and 3π/2. These four phase-shifted measurements form the standard four-step phase-shifting interferometry scheme for recovering the relative phase through quadra- ture combinations [13]. The resulting quadratures provide the wrapped relative phase and the interference modulation used to define a valid reconstruction region.

Fig. 5. Noise tolerance of the proposed wavefront sensor. Reconstruction error is evaluated as a function of additive measurement noise applied independently to the four phase- shifted interferograms.

Fig. 4. Inverse aberration recovery. The measured four-step interferometric data are used in an inverse forward-model op- timization to recover the exit-pupil aberration coefficients. De- focus, astigmatism, and spherical aberration are recovered as −2.00000, 3.00000, and 9.99998 waves, respectively, compared with the true values of −2, 3, and 10 waves. The resulting exit-pupil phase is reconstructed with an RMS phase error of < 10−6 rad, demonstrating accurate recovery of the imposed aberration.
